etymology: Hebrew Qedar, from a root meaning “dark” or “swarthy”; the second son of Ishmael, and the black-tented Arab tribes descended from him who ranged the northern deserts.
biblical_def: Kedar was the second son of Ishmael, and from him sprang the wandering Arab tribes whose black goat-hair tents darkened the wilderness pastures: “And these are the names of the sons of Ishmael…the firstborn of Ishmael, Nebajoth; and Kedar” (Gen 25:13). The psalmist, weary of dwelling among the fierce and the profane, cried, “Woe is me, that I sojourn in Mesech, that I dwell in the tents of Kedar” (Psa 120:5); and the bride of the Song owned her own dark comeliness, “black, but comely…as the tents of Kedar” (Son 1:5). Kedar stands for the sons of Ishmael, the wild man’s seed, ranging outside the covenant land, their glory measured by their flocks and their bowmen. Yet the LORD’s word ran even over these desert tribes: Isaiah pronounced that within a year all the glory of Kedar should fail (Isa 21:16), for no roving nation is beyond His reckoning. And the same prophet foresaw a better ingathering, when the flocks of Kedar should be gathered to the altar of the LORD to be accepted upon it (Isa 60:7). So Kedar preaches that the arm of grace reaches past the borders of Israel into the trackless desert, that the wandering sons of the bondwoman are not forgotten, and that the black tents of the wilderness shall yet yield worshippers to the God of Abraham, in whom all families of the earth are blessed.
webster_summary: The second son of Ishmael, and the black-tented Arab tribes descended from him (Gen 25:13; Psa 120:5); a witness that the LORD’s word and grace reach even the wandering desert nations.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sovereign reach of God over the nations that lie outside the covenant land. The wandering sons of the bondwoman are not beyond His word, for He decreed the failing of their glory, nor beyond His mercy, for He purposed that the flocks of Kedar be gathered to His altar and accepted. In Abraham’s seed all families of the earth are blessed, and the black tents of the desert shall yet yield worshippers.

etymology: Hebrew Tema, a son of Ishmael, and the desert oasis and tribe named for him in northern Arabia, a station on the caravan roads.
biblical_def: Tema was a son of Ishmael, numbered among the twelve princes of that stock: “Hadar, and Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah” (Gen 25:15). His name settled upon a desert oasis on the great caravan roads of Arabia, a place of wells and shade where the merchant trains rested and the thirsty found water. When Job likened his brethren’s failed comfort to a dried-up brook, he pictured the caravans reaching that oasis in vain: “The troops of Tema looked, the companies of Sheba waited for them” (Job 6:19), fainting because the water they trusted had failed. Yet the oasis could also answer the fugitive’s thirst, for Isaiah bids the men of Tema, “The inhabitants of the land of Tema brought water to him that was thirsty, they prevented with their bread him that fled” (Isa 21:14). Here is the parable of the wilderness: the world’s cisterns are broken and disappoint the caravans that look to them, but the LORD is a well that never fails. He calls to the very ends of the earth, “Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else” (Isa 45:22). The thirst of the desert is answered not by Tema’s cisterns, which may be dry, but by the fountain of living waters, who satisfies the fainting soul that flees to Him.
webster_summary: A son of Ishmael, and the desert oasis named for him whose caravans brought water to the thirsty (Gen 25:15; Isa 21:14); a parable of the wilderness thirst answered by the LORD.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the world’s wells are broken cisterns that fail the caravans who look to them, as the troops of Tema looked and were ashamed. The soul that flees the burning wilderness is not to trust the oasis of the flesh, which may be dry, but to look unto the LORD, who calls the ends of the earth to be saved and is Himself the fountain of living waters that never fails the thirsty.

etymology: Hebrew Midyan, “strife” or “contention”; a son of Abraham by Keturah, and the desert land east of the gulf where his descendants ranged.
biblical_def: Midian was a son of Abraham by Keturah, and the land east of the Red Sea gulf took his name and his roving tribes. Thither Moses fled from the wrath of Pharaoh: “But Moses fled from the face of Pharaoh, and dwelt in the land of Midian: and he sat down by a well” (Exo 2:15). At that well he found a wife and a flock, and forty years the future deliverer was schooled as a shepherd in the wilderness, learning at the backside of the desert to lead sheep before he led the LORD’s flock through it. Yet Midian was also a snare and a scourge. By Midianitish women Israel was drawn into whoredom and idolatry at Peor, one brazenly bringing a woman before the weeping congregation (Num 25:6); and in the days of the judges the LORD delivered His people into the hand of Midian seven years (Jdg 6:1), the Midianites and Amalekites and children of the east swarming up to devour the increase of the land (Jdg 6:3). Then the LORD raised Gideon and with three hundred men broke that vast host, so that ever after “the day of Midian” stood for God’s sudden shattering of the oppressor (Isa 9:4). So Midian teaches both mercies: the school where the LORD trains His shepherds, and the rod He breaks in a day when His people cry to Him.
webster_summary: A son of Abraham by Keturah, and the desert land of Moses’ exile and Gideon’s oppressor (Exo 2:15; Jdg 6:1); the school of the LORD’s shepherd and the scourge He shattered.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the double work of providence in the same place. Midian was the LORD’s quiet school, where He hid Moses forty years and made a prince into a shepherd; and Midian was the LORD’s rod, the scourge He raised to chastise Israel’s sin and then broke in a single night by Gideon’s little band. The God who trains His servants in the desert is the God who shatters the oppressor in the day of Midian when His people cry to Him.

etymology: Hebrew Ludim, a Hamitic people descended from Mizraim son of Ham; an African nation, distinct from the Shemite Lud son of Shem.
biblical_def: Ludim appears in the table of the nations as one of the peoples begotten of Mizraim, the son of Ham who is Egypt: “And Mizraim begat Ludim, and Anamim, and Lehabim, and Naphtuhim” (Gen 10:13). These are the African Ludim, a Hamitic stock sprung from Egypt, and they are to be distinguished from the Shemite Lud, brother of Elam and Asshur and Aram (Gen 10:22). Scripture names them among the mercenary bowmen of the nations, men of war hired to fill the ranks of the great trading powers. But the deeper doctrine of Ludim is the doctrine of the whole tenth of Genesis: every nation upon the face of the earth is reckoned from the three sons of Noah, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and not one people is fatherless or self-made. The sons of Ham are set down by name as surely as the sons of Shem, for “the sons of Ham; Cush, and Mizraim, and Phut, and Canaan” (Gen 10:6). God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26). The Ludim, like all the peoples, stand under one Judge and one promise, for in Abraham’s seed “shall all families of the earth be blessed” (Gen 12:3). The table of nations is the covenant’s wide horizon.
webster_summary: A Hamitic people descended from Mizraim, an African nation of bowmen (Gen 10:13), distinct from the Shemite Lud; a witness that all nations are reckoned from Noah under one Judge.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the unity and accountability of the whole human race. The tenth of Genesis names the peoples of the earth, sons of Ham no less than sons of Shem, and declares that God made of one blood all nations and set the bounds of their dwelling. There is no fatherless people and no self-made race; all stand under one Judge, and all are within the compass of the promise that in Abraham’s seed the families of the earth are blessed.

etymology: Hebrew Achzib, “lie” or “deceit”, from a root meaning to fail or deceive; a town in the lowland of Judah, distinct from Achzib of Asher on the coast.
biblical_def: Achzib of Judah was a town of the Shephelah, the lowland, listed among the cities of the tribe of Judah: “And Keilah, and Achzib, and Mareshah; nine cities with their villages” (Jos 15:44). It must be distinguished from the Achzib of Asher, a coastal town of the northern border; this is the inland Achzib of the south. Its very name preaches, for Achzib means “a lie” or “a deceit”, and the prophet Micah made a bitter pun upon it, declaring that “the houses of Achzib shall be a lie to the kings of Israel” (Mic 1:14), a deceiving brook that fails the traveller in the drought. So this little town becomes a sermon on false hope. Whatsoever the world offers to prop the kingdoms of men is a lie, a winter torrent that runs full when it is not needed and is dry when the thirsty come. Righteousness alone establishes a people, for “righteousness exalteth a nation: but sin is a reproach to any people” (Pro 14:34), and the nation whose God is the LORD is the only one truly blessed (Psa 33:12). All the boasted powers that are not built on Him are counted before Him “less than nothing, and vanity” (Isa 40:17). Achzib bids the soul forsake the deceiving cisterns of the world and rest upon the faithfulness of God, who cannot lie.
webster_summary: A town in the lowland of Judah whose name means “a lie” (Jos 15:44; Mic 1:14), distinct from Achzib of Asher; a sermon on the false hope of the world set against the faithfulness of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the emptiness of every hope that is not built on God. The name Achzib means a lie, a deceiving brook that fails the thirsty, and Micah made it a byword for the false confidences of the kings of Israel. Righteousness alone exalts a nation; the people whose God is the LORD alone are blessed; and all the powers that trust in themselves are less than nothing before Him. Forsake the deceiving cistern and rest on the faithful God who cannot lie.

etymology: Hebrew Botsrah, “sheepfold” or “fortress”, from a root meaning to enclose or fortify; a city of the plain of Moab, distinct from the famous Bozrah of Edom.
biblical_def: Bozrah of Moab was a fortified city of the Moabite plain, named among the towns brought under the prophet Jeremiah’s sweeping oracle of judgment: “And upon Kerioth, and upon Bozrah, and upon all the cities of the land of Moab, far or near” (Jer 48:24). It is to be distinguished from the more famous Bozrah of Edom, that red winepress of the LORD’s treading; this is the Moabite Bozrah, a stronghold beyond Jordan whose name, like Edom’s, means a fortress or an enclosed fold. Moab was the proud and settled nation, at ease from his youth, that had not been emptied from vessel to vessel, and therefore his taste remained in him and his scent was not changed. But the LORD had a controversy with the pride of Moab, and Jeremiah pronounced woe upon her cities far and near, that no fenced place should shelter her presumption. For “the LORD hath a controversy with the nations, he will plead with all flesh” (Jer 25:31), and before Him all nations are “counted…less than nothing, and vanity” (Isa 40:17). He shall famish the gods of the earth and be worshipped by men, every one from his place (Zep 2:11). Bozrah of Moab teaches that no wall is high enough and no fold strong enough to hide the pride of the nations from the judgment of God; every stronghold, far or near, must answer to Him.
webster_summary: A fortified city of Moab under Jeremiah’s judgment (Jer 48:24), distinct from Bozrah of Edom; a witness that no stronghold shelters the pride of the nations from the LORD.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no fortress shelters the pride of the nations from the judgment of God. Moab was at ease, settled and presumptuous, and trusted in her fenced places; but the LORD has a controversy with the nations and pleads with all flesh, and He named the cities of Moab, far or near, for the sword. Before Him the proudest peoples are less than nothing, and He will famish the gods of the earth. Let the strongholds of men not be trusted, but the LORD alone feared.

etymology: Greek Antipatris, a town on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea, rebuilt by Herod the Great and named in honour of his father Antipater.
biblical_def: Antipatris was a town upon the great road running down from Jerusalem to Caesarea by the sea, rebuilt by Herod the Great and named for his father Antipater. It enters Scripture at a single verse, yet a memorable one, for it was the night station of a Roman escort guarding the apostle Paul: “Then the soldiers, as it was commanded them, took Paul, and brought him by night to Antipatris” (Act 23:31). Forty Jewish assassins had bound themselves under a curse to kill him, but the plot was uncovered by a young kinsman, and the chief captain sent Paul away under cover of darkness with a great guard of horsemen and footmen. The whole march to Antipatris preaches the providence of God, who set a hedge of Roman spears about His servant that not one hair of his head should fall until his appointed work was done. The Lord had already stood by Paul the night before and said, “so must thou bear witness also at Rome”; and no ambush of forty men, no oath, no darkness could hinder that word. He who made of one blood all nations and “determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26) was directing every mile of that midnight ride. The heathen were promised for Christ’s inheritance and “the uttermost parts of the earth” for His possession (Psa 2:8); and to carry that gospel to Rome, God moved a garrison to guard one chained preacher.
webster_summary: A town on the Jerusalem-to-Caesarea road whither soldiers brought Paul by night, guarding him from ambush (Act 23:31); a witness to the providence that keeps God’s servant for his appointed work.

corruption_paragraphs: Antipatris is a plain waypoint on the coastal road, a Herodian town named for Antipater; the place bears no modern controversy, only the memory of a midnight march that saved an apostle’s life.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the particular providence of God over His servants. Forty men had sworn Paul’s death, yet the plot was uncovered by a boy and foiled by a garrison, and the apostle was borne safely by night to Antipatris. The Lord had said he must bear witness at Rome, and no oath or ambush could break that word. God, who fixed the bounds of the nations’ habitation, moved Roman spears to guard one chained preacher until his testimony was done.

etymology: Greek Kolossai, a city of Phrygia in the Lycus valley of Asia Minor, near Laodicea and Hierapolis; the church there received Paul’s epistle to the Colossians.
biblical_def: Colosse was a city of Phrygia in the valley of the river Lycus, once great upon the wool trade but by apostolic times overshadowed by its neighbours Laodicea and Hierapolis. Its name endures because a company of saints gathered there received one of Paul’s richest letters: “To the saints and faithful brethren in Christ which are at Colosse: Grace be unto you, and peace, from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Col 1:2). The apostle had not himself planted them; Epaphras had preached Christ to them, and the same Epaphras laboured in prayer for them and for the saints in Laodicea and Hierapolis (Col 4:13). To this little flock, threatened by a specious philosophy that would add angels, ordinances, and the traditions of men to Christ, Paul unfolded the surpassing glory and all-sufficiency of the Son. He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of every creature, before all things, and by Him all things consist; He is the head of the body, the church; and in Him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily. The whole epistle is a bulwark of the pre-eminence and sufficiency of Christ, teaching the saints that they are complete in Him and need no other. Colosse thus stands for every congregation, small and obscure, to whom the fulness of Christ is preached against every vain philosophy; and it points to the great multitude of “all nations, and kindreds, and people” (Rev 7:9) gathered at last before the Lamb.
webster_summary: A Phrygian city in the Lycus valley whose saints received Paul’s epistle (Col 1:2); the church to whom he unfolded the pre-eminence and all-sufficiency of Christ against every vain philosophy.

corruption_summary: The Phrygian church to whom Paul preached the fulness of Christ; the entry rebukes the vain philosophy and false teaching that Colossians was written to overthrow.
corruption_paragraphs: Colosse names a genuine corruption, for the epistle to that church was written against a real and dangerous error. A specious teaching had crept in that would join to Christ the worship of angels, the ordinances and traditions of men, a rigorous asceticism, and a philosophy after the rudiments of the world. It puffed up the flesh with a show of wisdom and humility while it detracted from the Head, as though the saints were not already complete in Him.

Against this Paul set the sword of Christ’s all-sufficiency: in the Son dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily, and the believer is complete in Him who is the head of all principality and power. The same error abides wherever men add to the finished work and full person of Christ the vain philosophy of the age, whether ancient angelology or modern speculation, spoiling the saints through “philosophy and vain deceit”. The remedy is unchanged: hold the Head, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and beware lest any man spoil you.

etymology: Greek Hierapolis, “sacred city”, from hieros, holy, and polis, city; a town of Phrygia above the Lycus, near Laodicea and Colosse, famed for its hot springs.
biblical_def: Hierapolis, whose name means “the sacred city”, stood upon the heights above the Lycus valley, crowned with terraces of white mineral springs, near its sister cities Laodicea and Colosse. Once a heathen city of shrines, it is named in Scripture only where the apostle bears record of a faithful minister’s labour for it: “For I bear him record, that he hath a great zeal for you, and them that are in Laodicea, and them in Hierapolis” (Col 4:13). That servant was Epaphras, a Colossian who had carried the gospel into that valley and who now, a prisoner’s companion at Rome, could not cease to strive for his people. Paul calls him one “always labouring fervently for you in prayers, that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God”; and the word rendered labouring is the word of an agonizing wrestler. Hierapolis therefore preaches the labour of prayer, the unseen toil of the faithful minister who, far from his flock and bound in chains, carries three churches upon his heart before the throne. It is a picture of the whole ministry of intercession, that a pastor’s hardest and holiest work is often done upon his knees for saints he cannot reach with his hands. The sacred city’s true holiness was not in its temples of stone but in the prayers of one man who wrestled that its believers might stand perfect and complete in the will of God.
webster_summary: A Phrygian city above the Lycus, near Laodicea and Colosse, for which Epaphras had great zeal (Col 4:13); a witness to the labour of prayer and the faithful minister striving for the saints.

corruption_summary: The Phrygian sacred city for which Epaphras strove in prayer; the entry recovers the labour of intercession and the faithful minister’s hidden toil for the saints.
corruption_paragraphs: Hierapolis, a heathen sacred city turned gospel ground, presses no modern quarrel upon the reader; it is remembered chiefly as one of the three churches carried on the heart of Epaphras.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the labour of prayer. Epaphras, though bound with the apostle far away at Rome, laboured fervently in his prayers for Hierapolis and her sister churches, that they might stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. The faithful minister’s hardest and holiest work is often unseen, done upon his knees for saints his hands cannot reach. The sacred city’s true holiness was in that wrestling intercession, not in its temples of stone.

etymology: Hebrew Migdol, “tower” or “watchtower”, from gadal, to be great; a frontier tower-city on the north-eastern border of Egypt, distinct from the Migdol of the Exodus encampment.
biblical_def: Migdol means “a tower”, and this Migdol was a fortress-town upon the north-eastern frontier of Egypt, a border watchtower where the fugitive remnant of Judah settled after they fled from the LORD’s appointed chastening. It is distinct from the Migdol of the Exodus, near which Israel encamped before the sea; this is the later frontier city where Jeremiah found the disobedient Jews: “The word that came to Jeremiah concerning all the Jews which dwell in the land of Egypt, which dwell at Migdol, and at Tahpanhes, and at Noph, and in the country of Pathros” (Jer 44:1). They had gone down into Egypt against the plain command of God, thinking to hide behind Pharaoh’s towers from the sword and famine they feared; but the prophet declared that the sword they dreaded should overtake them there. Ezekiel marked the whole reach of Egypt’s coming desolation from that same border tower to the far south: the land should be made waste “from the tower of Syene even unto the border of Ethiopia” (Eze 29:10), which the margin reads “from Migdol to Syene”. From the northern watchtower to the southern cataract, the whole length of Egypt lay open to the judging hand of the LORD. Migdol teaches that no frontier fortress, no borrowed strength of the nations, can shelter the disobedient from God; His arm reaches from Migdol to Syene, and there is no border where He is not.
webster_summary: A frontier tower-city on Egypt’s north-eastern border where fugitive Judah dwelt (Jer 44:1; Eze 29:10), distinct from the Exodus Migdol; a witness that no border escapes the LORD’s hand.

corruption_summary: The frontier tower-city of Egypt where disobedient Judah sheltered; the entry recovers that no border fortress hides the disobedient from the reach of the LORD’s hand.
corruption_paragraphs: Migdol in Egypt is a border fortress named by the prophets, clearly distinct from the Migdol of the Exodus route; the tower-town itself raises no modern controversy, only the warning it carried to fugitive Judah.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that no frontier or borrowed strength can shelter the disobedient from God. Judah fled into Egypt against His plain word, thinking to hide behind Pharaoh’s towers from the sword and famine they feared, and settled at Migdol on the border; but the LORD declared the sword should find them there. From Migdol on the north to Syene in the far south the whole land lay open to His judging hand. The nations are less than nothing before Him, and there is no border where He is not.
